book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House

chapters.relation: Fosl argues that Metallica's lyrics echo Nietzsche's and Marx's moral critiques of Christianity: songs like "Leper Messiah" and "The God that Failed" cast religion as slave-morality ressentiment, mind-control, and Marx's "opium of the people." He then asks whether the band achieves a Nietzschean transvaluation or lapses into the very nihilism Nietzsche said Christianity breeds — reading "To Live is to Die" and "One" as nostalgic death-wish, but "Escape" and "The Four Horsemen" as genuine defiant self-overcoming after the death of God.

Sharp maps Battlestar Galactica's Cylon uprising onto Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the enslaved Cylons, like Nietzsche's early Christians under Rome, invent a slave morality that inverts their masters' values, condemning human pride and greed while exalting a single loving God, souls, and equality. He shows Leoben preaching the soul to Starbuck and the Cylons' consensus-based commune as the powerless revaluing weakness into virtue, converting their polytheistic, master-moral human creators much as Christianity converted Rome.

chapters.file: ch33 - The Viewer and the Look.md
chapters.relation: Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.

chapters.file: ch34 - Determinism and the Dark Knight.md
chapters.relation: Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce Wayne with Angst and his own finitude, and — as in Miller's Year One, where a bat crashes through the window and he decides "I shall become a bat" — he authentically chooses his crime-fighting mission rather than being mechanically driven by trauma or vengeance.

chapters.file: ch35 - You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”.md
chapters.relation: Kyle contrasts House's detached, impartial "ethic of justice" with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care, drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, refuses to deceive patients, and attends to their social networks — letting parents hold their dying baby in "Maternity," defending Ezra's autonomy in "Informed Consent." But Kyle also presses the standard critique that valorizing care can cost the carer: Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment in "Acceptance" and pushes her toward Houselike tactics.

Mann reads Stephenie Meyer's Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" who orbits Edward like a satellite, valued only through the constant masculine gaze, embodying the adolescent girl's renunciation of her "I can" body. Mann finds a buried feminist subtext — Bella's desire, Edward's restraint, and her vampire transformation into a fierce, powerful equal — but ultimately faults Meyer for reinstating the old promise that a woman gains subjecthood through self-annihilation in a sovereign man's eyes.

chapters.file: ch37 - Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!.md
chapters.relation: Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.

chapters.file: ch39 - Gaining Trust from the Past.md
chapters.relation: Davies analyzes Lost's Oceanic 815 survivors as a genuine state of nature, playing off the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. He distinguishes Rousseau's compassionate "Innocence" from a Hobbesian "Trust No. 1" (Sawyer hoarding), tracks "tragedies of the commons" over water and Shannon's inhalers, and Jack and Sayid's move toward Lockean punishment and civil society. Using game theory's prisoners' dilemma and tit-for-tat, he argues cooperation emerges when survivors, discovering the Others, resolve to "act as one body" and form a commonwealth.

Bray argues the American Office does depict class — precisely as a "salaried mass" whose identity rests on denying class difference. Using Marx's account of surplus value and alienated, deskilled labor (Stanley's "run-out-the-clock" situation, Pam's deadened art), he shows the office as a site of exploitation Michael Scott cannot properly manage. Michael's condo, the ex-convict comparing prison to Dunder-Mifflin, and Ryan's ambitions expose the gap between self-image and reality; via Walter Benjamin, Bray locates "authentic humanity" in that very tension.

O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.

Pierce asks whether the X-Men's mutants are a race. Drawing on Appiah's data that racial groups are not genetically distinct enough to be biological subspecies, he shows mutants — diverse in origin and mutation, sharing only an X-Gene that non-mutants also carry — are even less a biological race. Turning to socially-constructed race, he uses Days of Future Past's camps and Genosha's mutant slavery (the "Genejoke" slur, gene-testing) to argue mutants are racelike and could become a social race, though strictly they are only an analogy for racial oppression.

chapters.file: ch44 - “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons.md
chapters.relation: McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.

Ruff and Barris argue that House's rude, rule-breaking rhetoric works like a Zen koan: by insisting "everybody lies" and unsettling everyone's (and his own) habitual sense-making, he opens space for the true problem to reveal itself. Through cases like "DNR," "Mob Rules," and "House vs. God," they show his refusal of justification is a way of acting ethically, establishing naked intimacy, reaching truth, and healing — all one nondual "happening." House is inside the rhetoric, performed by it, ending each case in Zen-like equanimity amid personal chaos.

chapters.file: ch46 - Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat.md
chapters.relation: White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.

chapters.file: ch49 - House and the Life of Reason.md
chapters.relation: Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
